title: The £30 Demob Gratuity Jack Cohen Spent on a Hackney Barrow
dek: Home from the war in 1919, a tailor's son refused his father's workshop and put everything he had into surplus food and a market pitch.

story.event: Spending his demobilisation gratuity on surplus food and trading from a barrow in Well Street Market, Hackney
story.summary: In 1919 Jack Cohen, a tailor's son from Whitechapel just demobilised from the Royal Flying Corps, refused to return to his father's workshop and spent his £30 gratuity on surplus forces food, which he sold from a barrow in Well Street Market, Hackney. He worked London's street markets six days a week, began selling tea under the Tesco name in 1924 and opened his first shops in the early 1930s.
paragraphs: In 1919 Jack Cohen came home to east London from the Royal Flying Corps. Born in Whitechapel in 1898, the son of Avroam Kohen, a tailor from Łódź, he had left school at fourteen to work in his father's business and had not liked it. His war had taken him to France, Egypt and Palestine, making canvas for balloons and aircraft. In December 1917, the Jewish Chronicle records, the requisitioned ship he was aboard struck a mine in Alexandria harbour, and a nurse pulled him from the water.

Back in London his father's trade was waiting, and Cohen told him he would not go back to tailoring. What he had instead was a demobilisation gratuity of £30. What was cheap was food the forces no longer needed, surplus stock of the NAAFI, the services' canteen organisation. He spent the gratuity on it and took a barrow to Well Street Market in Hackney, one trader among dozens of stalls.

An Irish Examiner retelling in 2004 put the profit of his first day at £1. The Jewish Chronicle lists his early stock as army surplus, fish paste and golden syrup, and a Kent Online history says he sold whatever he could salvage, sanding the rust off tins of fruit. Traders raced each morning for the best pitches; Cohen, the Chronicle recounts, won his by throwing his cap. English Heritage records that he became a costermonger, working a different London market every day except Sunday, and that his low prices and fast turnover earned him the name "Jack the Slasher".

In 1924 he married Sarah "Cissie" Fox, and their wedding-present money went into a wholesale business. Around then he began selling packets of tea bought from a supplier, T. E. Stockwell, under a name made from Stockwell's initials and the first two letters of Cohen: Tesco. The first Tesco shops, at Becontree and Burnt Oak, opened in the early 1930s, and by 1939 there were about a hundred around London. His motto stayed the market's: "pile it high, sell it cheap."

quote.text: it would be hard to find a work which did not involve some liability to account; in fact it is difficult to do anything without some mistake or other
quote.source_title: The Memorabilia, tr. Henry Graham Dakyns, Project Gutenberg eBook #1177
quote.connection: Socrates says this to Eutherus, another man home from a war, who will not take work in which he must answer to someone else. Cohen escaped his father's workshop, yet on a barrow every passing shopper held him to account, daily and without notice.

reflection: It is easy to think a real start needs more than you have: more money, more certainty, a proper shop. Cohen's first stock was food the army no longer wanted, and his first premises were a barrow among dozens. The shops came more than a decade later.

Socrates' point is worth keeping beside that story. Leaving his father's workshop did not free Cohen from judgement; it handed the judging to strangers who could walk to the next stall. Working on your own terms still means answering to someone, often many people, and that can tire you as much as it frees you. Both things can be true on the same morning.
invitation: Name one person your work answers to this week, a customer, a colleague or someone at home. Ask them one question about what would make it easier for them, and simply write down the answer.

research_notes: Age: the Jewish Chronicle, the Irish Examiner and Hackney Council say he was 21 when he started in 1919; the Hackney Gazette says 20. He was born in October 1898, so either is possible depending on the month; the story gives his birth year and no age. Service: English Heritage and the Chronicle say Royal Flying Corps; the Irish Examiner says RAF (the RFC became the RAF in April 1918), so the story uses the RFC. First-day takings: only the Irish Examiner (2004) among the sources that load gives a first-day figure (£1 profit); an Internet Archive copy of The Grocer's 'Tesco's defining moments' (a promotional feature) gives £1 profit on £4 of sales, and a Telegraph history is said to give the same, but the first is paid content and the second could not be read, so neither is cited and the story gives only the £1, naming the Examiner. Goods: English Heritage says surplus NAAFI foodstuffs; the Chronicle adds fish paste and golden syrup; the Kent Online detail of sanding rust off tins is attributed to it. First shops: English Heritage says Tesco Stores Ltd was registered in 1932 and the first shops opened at Becontree and Burnt Oak; other accounts give 1929 or September 1931 for Burnt Oak; the story says 'early 1930s'. The Tesco name: English Heritage and Hackney Museum describe tea bought from T. E. Stockwell; the Chronicle dates the brand to 1924, so the story says 'around then'. The cap-throwing and the Osmanieh rescue rest on the Chronicle's 2019 profile and are attributed to it; the Chronicle itself flags the wedding-present story as 'the story', and English Heritage states it plainly. Tesco's own history page renders by script and was not used. Quote: Socrates' conversation with Eutherus, who has returned from abroad at the close of the Peloponnesian War with his foreign property lost and nothing from his father, and who refuses a steward's post because he will not be held to account; it is applied to Cohen by analogy.
